title: Trump Approves 30-Year Nuclear Deal Allowing Saudi Arabia to Enrich Uranium
excerpt: The landmark agreement, worth tens of billions of dollars, would give American companies a central role in Saudi Arabia's nuclear program while opening the door to uranium enrichment on Saudi soil under a secretive arrangement.
body:
• President Trump has formally approved a 30-year nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia worth tens of billions of dollars, with Energy Secretary Chris Wright expected to sign it Wednesday.
  • The deal could allow uranium enrichment on Saudi soil under a secretive "black box" arrangement built and operated by American companies, pending a two-year feasibility study.
  • Saudi Arabia will not be required to adopt the IAEA's "gold standard" Additional Protocol for inspections, departing from the precedent set by the UAE's 2009 nuclear cooperation deal.
  • Congress must review the agreement, which critics warn risks accelerating nuclear proliferation across the Middle East amid the ongoing US-Iran war.

President Donald Trump has formally approved a landmark nuclear agreement with Saudi Arabia that would provide the kingdom with a civilian nuclear program and potentially allow uranium enrichment on its soil, reshaping decades of American nonproliferation policy.

The 30-year deal, first reported by The Wall Street Journal, is estimated to be worth tens of billions of dollars. It gives American companies a central role in developing Saudi Arabia's nuclear infrastructure while shutting out competitors including Russia and China. Energy Secretary Chris Wright is expected to sign the accord on Wednesday alongside Saudi counterpart Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman.

Under the agreement, new power reactors and other nuclear technology would be provided by American companies, with Westinghouse Electric and its AP1000 reactor — capable of producing about 1,100 megawatts of electricity — positioned as the biggest beneficiary.

The Enrichment Question

The deal's most consequential provision centers on uranium enrichment. A joint US-Saudi team would conduct a two-year study to examine whether it would be commercially viable to enrich uranium on Saudi soil instead of relying on imported fuel. If the study concludes enrichment is warranted, Americans would build the facility under a secretive "black box" arrangement that would preclude the transfer of sensitive enrichment technology to Riyadh.

If the US ultimately objects to proceeding with enrichment, the kingdom would be barred from carrying it out on its own or with another foreign partner for 10 years. The deal also bars Riyadh from developing its own enrichment technology or purchasing it from other countries during that period, according to the Journal.

Saudi officials have long argued the deal is necessary to develop a nuclear industry that would draw on unproven domestic uranium ore deposits to meet energy needs, freeing up more oil production for export.

Safeguards Under Scrutiny

The agreement has already drawn sharp criticism over its inspection provisions. Unlike the United Arab Emirates, which signed a "gold standard" nuclear cooperation deal with the US in 2009, Saudi Arabia will not be required to adopt the International Atomic Energy Agency's Additional Protocol — a framework that allows for more rigorous monitoring and inspections.

The Saudis rejected the Additional Protocol over concerns that it could theoretically allow inspectors to enter the holy city of Mecca or royal palaces. Instead, the deal includes a bilateral safeguards agreement that resembles the model protocol but lacks the provisions that offended Riyadh, according to CNN. The IAEA Board of Governors will have to ratify its terms.

"The agreement could help revitalize the U.S. nuclear industry, strengthen U.S.-Saudi ties and deny Russia and China a strategically important role in the Saudi nuclear program. But unless it contains adequate constraints, including on enrichment, it could increase nuclear proliferation risks in the Middle East and beyond."

— Robert Einhorn, former senior State Department nonproliferation official

Alexander Bollfrass, a nuclear expert at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, called the deal "a revolutionary new approach" to nuclear nonproliferation policy, noting the US is willing to transfer highly sensitive technology without the standard level of internationally monitored safeguards.

Congressional Battle Ahead

The Trump administration is expected to submit the deal to Congress for review in the coming days, where it faces bipartisan opposition. However, blocking it would be difficult — an override of a presidential veto would require a two-thirds majority vote in both the House and Senate.

"A President waging war to prevent nuclear proliferation in the Middle East should not facilitate proliferation just because U.S. companies stand to make a profit."

— Rep. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.)

The deal arrives amid the ongoing US-Iran conflict, creating what critics call an awkward contradiction: the Trump administration is pressuring Tehran to curtail its nuclear program while helping Saudi Arabia develop one. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman has said that if Iran ever develops a nuclear weapon, his nation would follow suit.

Henry Sokolski, executive director of the Nonproliferation Policy Education Center, warned of broader consequences. "Whither goes Saudi Arabia, so goes the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Egypt. The idea that this will have a happy ending is delusional," he said.

Regional Stakes for the Indian Diaspora

The deal carries implications for the roughly 2.5 million Indian nationals living and working in Saudi Arabia, as any shift in the kingdom's geopolitical posture reverberates through the Gulf's economic ecosystem. India, which forged its own civilian nuclear agreement with the US in 2008, has watched the Saudi negotiations closely — both as a regional stakeholder and as a country with deep ties to the Gulf states.

What Comes Next

Wright framed the agreement in expansive terms. "Thanks to President Trump, the American nuclear renaissance is underway and will deliver long-term benefits to the American and Saudi people," he said in a statement. Nuclear stocks rallied this week, with companies like Constellation Energy, Oklo, and NuScale Power climbing on the news.

The Biden administration had previously conditioned a similar nuclear deal on Saudi Arabia normalizing relations with Israel — an effort that collapsed after Hamas's October 2023 attack. Trump has not insisted on that linkage, effectively decoupling nuclear cooperation from the broader diplomatic agenda.

Congress now faces a stark choice: accept a deal that could reshape the nuclear landscape of the Middle East, or attempt the uphill fight of blocking a president's foreign policy initiative during wartime.
